**Moonlight Sonata**
Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 14 in C-sharp minor, subtitled "quasi una fantasia." Its first movement, an Adagio sostenuto, repeats soft G-sharp–C-sharp–E triplets and is played "senza sordino," with the sustain pedal held down. The critic Ludwig Rellstab compared it to moonlight on Lake Lucerne. Liszt called the D-flat major second movement "a flower between two abysses," and the Presto agitato finale races through C-sharp minor arpeggios. Chopin's Fantaisie-Impromptu is often said to echo it.

**Beethoven's 32 piano sonatas**
The "New Testament" of the piano repertoire. Nicknamed sonatas include the "Pathétique," "Waldstein," "Appassionata," "Les Adieux" (with "Lebewohl" written over its opening chords), and the huge "Hammerklavier," which Liszt premiered in public. The last, No. 32 in C minor, ends with a syncopated "Arietta" that Jeremy Denk called "proto-jazz." Artur Schnabel made the first complete recording.

**Mozart's piano sonatas and "Rondo alla turca"**
Mozart wrote 18 piano sonatas. No. 11 in A major ends with the "Rondo alla turca," which imitates Turkish Janissary bands with a "B–A–G-sharp–A–C" theme. The easy C major "Sonata facile" ("for beginners") opens over an Alberti bass, and the A minor sonata K. 310 was written around the time his mother died.

**Mozart's piano concertos and "Twinkle" variations**
Mozart wrote 27 piano concertos (counting early arrangements), including the E-flat concerto K. 271, which Alfred Einstein called Mozart's "Eroica." His twelve variations on "Ah vous dirai-je, Maman," the tune of "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star," were also written for piano.

**Thelonious Monk**
The bebop pianist called the "genius of modern music." He composed "'Round Midnight" and "Straight, No Chaser" and is known for saying the piano "ain't got no wrong notes."

**Dave Brubeck and "Take Five"**
The Dave Brubeck Quartet's album Time Out used unusual time signatures, as in "Take Five" (in 5/4, written by saxophonist Paul Desmond) and "Blue Rondo à la Turk." Brubeck's Jazz Impressions of Japan includes a track in which the piano imitates a koto.

**Herbie Hancock**
A jazz pianist and keyboardist who wrote "Watermelon Man" (re-recorded on his jazz-funk album Head Hunters) and "Cantaloupe Island" (from Empyrean Isles).

**Chick Corea, Keith Jarrett, and other jazz pianists**
Chick Corea founded the fusion band Return to Forever, recorded Light as a Feather, and wrote the standard "Spain." Keith Jarrett's improvised Köln Concert is a best-selling solo piano album. Other jazz pianists include Bill Evans, composer of "Waltz for Debby," and Joe Zawinul, who co-founded Weather Report with Wayne Shorter and wrote "Birdland."

**Frédéric Chopin and the "Minute Waltz"**
The Polish composer and pianist who wrote almost entirely for solo piano. His Waltz in D-flat major, the "Minute Waltz," was supposedly inspired by a little dog chasing its own tail.

**Famous piano concertos and competitions**
Nikolai Rubinstein at first harshly criticized Tchaikovsky's Piano Concerto No. 1, which later became a favorite. Rachmaninoff's Second Piano Concerto opens with bell-like chords, and his famously difficult Third, in D minor, has an optional harder "ossia" cadenza and was premiered in New York; Yunchan Lim played it to win the 2022 Van Cliburn Competition. Ravel's G major concerto opens with a whip crack, and his Concerto for the Left Hand was written for Paul Wittgenstein, who lost his right arm in World War I. Van Cliburn and Martha Argerich are famous winners of major piano competitions.

**Spanish piano music**
Isaac Albéniz's suite Iberia opens with "Evocación," and Alicia de Larrocha made a celebrated complete recording of it. Enrique Granados's Goyescas includes "The Maiden and the Nightingale," which reportedly inspired "Bésame Mucho." Manuel de Falla's Nights in the Gardens of Spain, for piano and orchestra, begins "In the Generalife" and was premiered by Ricardo Viñes.

**John Cage: prepared piano and 4′33″**
Cage invented the "prepared piano," in which screws, bolts, and rubber are placed between the strings, and used it in his Sonatas and Interludes, inspired by the Indian rasas. His 4′33″, conceived after a visit to an anechoic chamber, has three movements all marked "tacet," so the pianist sits silently at the instrument.

**Erik Satie**
A French composer of hypnotic piano pieces, including the three Gymnopédies and the Gnossiennes. He answered critics who called his music formless with Three Pieces in the Shape of a Pear, for piano four hands.

**Debussy's "Clair de lune" and the sustain pedal**
The third movement of Debussy's Suite bergamasque, which relies on the right-foot sustain (damper) pedal to blur its harmonies. Debussy's other piano works include the Preludes (such as "The Girl with the Flaxen Hair") and Children's Corner.

**Etudes**
Piano studies that teach technique. Famous sets include Liszt's 12 Transcendental Etudes (with "Mazeppa" and "Feux follets") and his Paganini Etudes (with "La Campanella"). Others are Bartók's 153 progressively harder Mikrokosmos pieces, which end with "Six Dances in Bulgarian Rhythm," Ligeti's etudes such as "The Devil's Staircase," and Conlon Nancarrow's Studies for Player Piano.
